lines: On my right is Kenneth Roth. Ken is the executive director of human rights watch He has been here for the last four days, meeting with many government officials, NGO activists, victims-survivors of many human rights violations in Indonesia. To my next is Mr Haris Azhar. Haris is the coordinator, the national coordinator of KontraS

Arguably Indonesia most influential human rights organization human rights organization We have known, Human Rights Watch and KontraS have known each other since.. I think since the very first establishment of KontraS. So please Ken, Ken will start the presentation, the talk, after that Haris will do.

Good morning everybody. It's a pleasure to be back in Jakarta. The subject of this morning's press conference is the question of what to do about the 1965 killings. You know why do these still matter to today's Indonesia and how can we properly address them. Obviously the murder at least half a million people in the course of just a few months

is one of the most horrendous crimes of our era and certainly of indonesia's history. This is a crime of such a magnitude that it cannot be swept under the rug. Families remember, you know survivors remember, the descendants remember. And they are bearing a scar, wound, that they want addressed.

This is also relevant for today, and this is not simply a matter of ancient history. I mean it's relevant because Indonesia remains a society in a country of many divisions. There are religious differences, ethnic differences, territorial differences. And a big question for Indonesia today is how does one bridge those differences.

1965 represents a terrible precedent for how to address differences. It represents a precedent of forcing those differences away, through mass murder. And sadly that is a precedent that because Indonesia has not really addressed it remains an option, remains alive possibility. And clearly this is an ugly episode in indonesia's history which we want never ever to repeat.

But the way to inoculate society against a recurrence of these atrocities is to openly address them, tell the truth about them acknowledge them, have justice where possible, and then move forward. But trying to forget the past, trying to suppress the past, to censor the past is the kind of thing that may condemn Indonesia to repeating the past.

And we think it's extremely important that a different approach be taken. Now I should stress that even though I speak here as the representative of an international human rights organization, this is not an international or foreign demand. This is an Indonesian demand. I have heard in the course of my visit and and my colleague Andreas is heard thru many many years of work here

that the deep desire to address these horrendous crimes is felt passionately and urgently by many Indonesians obviously by the survivors, obviously by the families but also by many ordinary Indonesians who may not have been personally touched by the killings but who nonetheless want to build a society founded on the truthful acknowledgement of the past

and a determination on the basis of knowledge not forgetting that we're gonna to move forward and never repeat that kind of lawlessness. This is a deeply indigenous, a deeply national demand. This is nothing to do with foreign desires. Now next week as I think many of you know the government is hosting a symposium on this topic

that is why frankly we are addressing this this issue today even though it is an issue that is now half a century old. This is a very important first step and we want to acknowledge a recognition that the government is taking a step toward a new approach It is not repeating the forgetfulness of the past It is making an initial effort to address the past.

And we applaud this important first step by the government. There are several options on the table as to what can be done . I want to begin with one that is clearly not imminent but it's important to recognize nonetheless and that is the option of justice. When you have crimes of this magnitude when you have mass murder involving hundreds of thousands of people, if not more

It is important ultimately for the architects of this slaughter to be brought to justice. It's never possible in a situation that involves so many people to bring the day to day murderers to account that's an unfortunate practical reality. I'm also aware that fifty years later it's not clear how many people are still alive. In a particularly among the leadership.

And this may be a situation like Eastern Europe where the most responsible individuals are no longer alive. So there may be you know important practical limits to the Justice option but I want to put that on the table because ideally you do bring to justice the architects the directors, the people who really oversaw this mass killing.

A second goal that will be discussed I don't think the Justice one will be actively discussed at the symposium but a second one that will actively be discussed is what's been termed rehabilitation. And here the references is to the 1981 so-called clean environment decree that had been issued by president Suharto.

I think as you all know, this was an efforts to cleanse the government bureaucracy particularly the security forces of anybody with a family history links to the PKI. And this is a group of people that has been said to involve some forty million Indonesians who today are barred from various forms of government employment in the civil service in the police and the army.

This is obviously a deep injustice.This is a classic example of collective punishment. And these are people who have never done anything wrong. They may have had a grandparent or a great grandparent who allegedly was affiliated with the PKI Ending this practice of blacklisting these people is obviously an important step.

And something that frankly the sooner the better There is no need to have a lengthy process. This is a decree that could be reversed with another decree. And we would like to see that happen and clearly the organizers of the symposium are interested in this. And that's a a good initial step when they can show up quick action.

The more difficult issue comes to the broader questions of how do you address these past atrocities. And and there is clearly interest in some kind of an apology in some kind of compensation and in you know a process of reconciliation. Now those are all good things. The question is when do they happen.

In particular do they happened before or after the process of telling the truth about the past. And in our view you can't apologize over a blank slate. You can't reconcile around censorship. You can't be compensated for a closed-door. What is needed is to begin with a truth-telling process.

To begin with an opportunity for the survivors perhaps for some of the participants for the descendants to speak publicly to offer their public testimony so that the Indonesian people can hear thesefirst-hand accounts This kind of public hearing process would lay a factual basis for what we presume with an ultimately be a some kind of truth commission report.

And when that has happened then it is possible for the government to acknowledge what has happened. You know then it's possible for the government to express its sorrow for what happened to apologize. You know then it's possible for the government to compensate the victims or their descendants. Those that are meaningful actions on the basis of a factual record.

They're not meaningful on the basis of a closed information environment. So we in assessing the results of the symposium are going to be looking in particular at whether there is the initiation of a real meaningful public truth-telling process. That is the sine-qua-non of an effective accountability process.

Now the final thing I'd like to mention is the role of the United States in this There are clearly our archives in the US governments records about what happened in 1965. There's been some policy level disclosures of a broad public statements. But that's not what we're really interested in.

We want to know the working-level involvement between the US government and the killers in 1965 Who knew what, what were the channels of communication. Were there names conveyed by the US government to the Indonesian government and if so what happened to those people It's this kind of operational detail.

The cables, the diplomatic messages, the CIA messages. That's what, it would be very useful to know as part of the effort to tell the history of 1965. This is not a substitute for an Indonesian process, this is really just one part of a broader picture. But nonetheless we feel that the US government could constructively contributes to a truth-telling process by opening up its archives and releasing to the public whatever communications exists there.

Now this is something that the US government has done in other cases. And so far always in Latin America. President Obama himself has opened up the archives with respect to the so-called dirty wars that took place in Brazil and Argentina. His predecessors as president have opened the archives with respect to Chile, El Salvador and Guatemala,

These have been very useful contributions to truth-telling processes in those countries. Now what seems to be a kind of a practical or political correctness it to the US doing this to the president being able to overcome the expectable bureaucratic resistance particularly in the CIA

to opening up the archives is that there needs to be a formal request from the government in question and a meaningful truth-telling process. Now in the case of Indonesia, Komnas HAM has made that request and that's a very important thing that has happened In our meetings with the government we have urged the government itself to add its voice requesting that the US government to open its archives.

Similarly we hope that the symposium launches a process that will enable the US government to see that there is a real truth-telling process underway in Indonesia and that the release of the US archives would make a contribution to an ongoing sincere genuine truth-telling process

If that happens if there really is a clear Indonesian government requests and if it is pursuant to a truth-telling process, we are confident that President Obama will do the right thing and open up the archives as he is done in other cases. We realize that there is resistance and that you know the army, the NU, are not eager for a

truth-telling process to go forward And frankly this is where Indonesian civil society has a role to play. The more the press clamors for a truth-telling process the more civil society joins in the more that president Jokowi is going to have the political backing needed to overcome this resistance

and to move forward both in telling the truth here in Indonesia and also requesting the assistance of the US government and others to open up their archives and to contribute their part of this historical record. So we see next week as the beginning of what we hope is a historic moment.

An effort to really come to terms with this ugly period of Indonesia's past and to move forward in a way that no longer sweeps this matter under the rug but reveals as fully as possible what happened acknowledges it And build the foundation of the rule of law. So that there is a much lesser chance that Indonesia will ever repeat this terrible period in its past.
